stories.headline: Noel Tata Hits Back With New Merger Plan | Can Tata Sons Avoid Listing? | Boardroom War
stories.title: Noel Tata Hits Back With New Merger Plan | Can Tata Sons Avoid Listing? | Boardroom War
stories.summary: The Tata Sons boardroom battle has taken a dramatic new turn as Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata proposes a major restructuring to keep the Tata Group's holding company unlisted. The proposal seeks to merge two operating businesses with Tata Sons, potentially changing its regulatory classification and removing the requirement for a stock market listing. But why was this option not explored earlier? Sources tracking the developments tell Business Today TV that the proposal raises serious questions about the board's previous decisions. The latest move follows a contentious boardroom vote in which four directors supported N Chandrasekaran's reappointment, Noel Tata opposed it, and Chandrasekaran abstained. With the RBI's regulatory position, reported government intervention and an approaching Annual General Meeting adding to the uncertainty, the stakes remain high. Watch this Business Today TV special report for the proposal, the boardroom confrontation and what could happen next in this corporate battle.

stories.headline: No bar on conducting byelection in Perundurai, Election Commission tells Madras High Court
stories.title: No bar on conducting byelection in Perundurai, Election Commission tells Madras High Court
stories.summary: It, however, adds that bypolls to Tiruchi East, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai and Karur will have to wait till disposal of connected election petitions
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The legal bar for conduct of byelections in Perundurai Assembly constituency has ended due to the rejection of an election petition related to that constituency on September 8, 2026, the Election Commission of India (EC) has submitted before the Madras High Court.

In its written submissions filed in response to a public interest litigation petition pending before Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan, the EC said the Perundurai bypoll could be conducted before November 24, 2026 if the Supreme Court does not grant any stay.

The EC said the conduct of bypoll would also be subject to the Chief Justice’s Bench exempting Perundurai from an interim order passed by it on July 10, 2026 restraining the commission from notifying bypolls to five vacant constituencies with respect to which election petitions were pending in the High Court.

In so far as the other four constituencies -- Tiruchi East, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai and Karur -- were concerned, the EC said the byelections cannot be notified to them until the election petitions, filed along with a plea to declare either those petitioners or other candidates as returned candidates, were decided.

Though Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who had vacated Tiruchi East and retained Perambur after winning from both the seats in the general elections, had contended that he resigned even before the filing of an election petition by DMK candidate S. Inigo Irudayaraj, the EC said the timing of the resignation was immaterial.

The Commission said it would not matter whether an election petition was filed either before or after the resignation because either way a constituency might end up facing an anomalous situation of being represented by two individuals if someone else gets declared as returned candidate by the election tribunal (High Court) after the conduct of bypolls.

Claiming that the deferment of bypolls was “neither indefinite nor indiscriminate,” the EC said the bar would come to an end immediately after the election tribunal disposes of a plea made along with an election petition to declare either the petitioner or some other candidate as returned candidate.

“This has already happened for Perundurai constituency,” the Commission said, and underlined that Section 86(7) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 requires every election petition to be disposed of as expeditiously as possible with an endeavour to conclude the trial within six months.
“The Commission fully recognises the importance of every constituency being represented...
The Commission would welcome any direction this court considers appropriate for the expeditious disposal ofthe pending election petitions,” the EC’s written submissions read.

stories.headline: ‘Major food crisis’ looming : Jaishankar
stories.title: ‘Major food crisis’ looming : Jaishankar
stories.summary: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has warned of an impending “major food crisis” in the coming months, compounding severe global fertiliser shortages triggered by ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and West Asia. Speaking during a conversation hosted at the Asia Society on Monday, Jaishankar highlighted the severe strain these geopolitical tensions are placing on Global South economies, describing the overall situation as “very very stressful.”“… this is a big concern for us, which is, if you look at these two conflicts, the Ukraine and now the Iran-Gulf conflict, they've actually had a devastating impact on Global South economies,” Jaishankar noted.Addressing the growing volatility in energy markets, Jaishankar emphasized that global supply chains are under double pressure from both physical insecurity and diplomatic maneuvering. He cautioned that political interference during a period of tight market conditions risks driving up fuel prices when stabilization is urgently needed.Also read: Siang project not just hydropower, vital for national security: Arunachal Pradesh CM Pema Khandu“So part of it is actually the security of oil supplies, and part of it is the politics of oil supplies, and they are feeding into each other, and they are creating a double crisis or an aggravated crisis,” he explained, adding that if “people play politics with it, that adds to the complications in the market.”The Minister expressed acute concern over agricultural inputs and grain shipments, pointing to disrupted maritime corridors and impacted production centers in key regions."We are today looking at a situation where some of the major grain exporters will not be able to send out their shipments, particularly out to the Black Sea," Jaishankar stated.He further noted that global fertiliser production has been heavily disrupted because key producers are situated in West Asia and Russia. Coupled with severe climate disruptions, the cascading impacts threaten global food security.Also read: NCERT's new Class 9 textbook highlights anecdotes of lesser-known women rulers in Indian historyCombined with impacts of climate patterns like a super El Nino, Jaishankar said, “there is going to be a major food crisis probably in the coming months. So if you have energy as a big crunch, and then food and fertilisers on top of it, and finance because every time there's a conflict, money moves towards safe harbours and away from the Global South, the net result of it has been really very very stressful.”Critiquing narrow geopolitical decision-making, Jaishankar insisted that major powers cannot dismiss the unintended fallout of their actions on developing nations.“Countries should not be so self-centred that you're in your own world and take your decision and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’,” he remarked, stressing that “sound common sense” should ensure the basic needs of vulnerable countries are not neglected to the point of acute distress. “And that is a concern that we have.”Jaishankar warned that energy shortages inevitably lead to broader economic and political volatility, drawing parallels to recent shifts in South Asia. “We have already seen it after the Ukraine war. We saw in our neighbourhood the direct result of that in political instability, and my fear is what is happening in Iran and the Gulf is going to feed, is going to aggravate,” he cautioned.Regarding how developing nations will navigate these escalating pressures, Jaishankar pointed out that responses will vary depending on national resilience and autonomy.“Some others would find it harder to do so. So those of us who are autonomous, we'd like to see more of us who are autonomous. But it’s not a black and white scenario. It would depend on the issue and the stakes involved. There'll be cases where countries would make adjustments. There'll be cases where they would fight back,” he said.

stories.title: Supreme Court Questions High Medicine Prices At Corporate Hospitals | Essential Drugs Pricing
stories.summary: The Supreme Court has raised serious concerns over the pricing of essential medicines at corporate hospitals, questioning why patients are often required to purchase drugs through in-house pharmacies at significantly higher prices. The bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandip Mehta has sought answers from the government and the healthcare sector on the gap between retailer prices and MRP. stories.headline: Supreme Court Grants Bail To Man Accused Of Making Objectionable Posts Against Jharkhand CM's Wife Kalpana Soren
stories.title: Supreme Court Grants Bail To Man Accused Of Making Objectionable Posts Against Jharkhand CM's Wife Kalpana Soren
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court today granted bail to a 30-year-old security guard challenging the Jharkhand High Court's refusal to grant him bail in a case arising from allegedly obscene and derogatory Facebook posts against Jharkhand Chief Minister Hemant Soren's wife, Kalpana Soren, who is a sitting MLA from Gandey.

A bench of Justice M.M. Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B. Varale observed that he has been incarcerated for over a year and the maximum sentence prescribed for the offences against him is three years imprisonment.
The Court opined that custodial interrogation is not required.
Before the Supreme Court, Uraon has argued that the High Court failed to properly consider his prolonged custody and the stage of the proceedings.
His plea states that the investigation has been completed and the chargesheet has been filed.
It further says that the prosecution's case rests on electronic evidence already in its possession and that there is no requirement for his continued custody.

The plea further contends that the High Court rejected bail solely on the seriousness of the offence, which cannot be the sole ground for denying bail and as the court must consider the overall facts and circumstances.

The petitioner has also pointed out that he was granted bail in another case arising from the same alleged incident based on a complaint by Javed Ansari, the head of the Kanke Block Coordination Committee, on February 13, 2026.
He contends that the two cases arose from the same offence and that the High Court failed to give due consideration to his custody since September 6, 2025.
The plea also points out that neither case was registered at the instance of Kalpana Soren herself.
The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the State of Jharkhand on his plea against the High Court's bail rejection.
The petitioner was represented by Advocate Rahul Shyam Bhandari.

stories.title: Supreme Court Collegium Recommends Repatriation Of Justice T Vinod Kumar To Telangana HC Ahead Of Retirement
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court Collegium has recommended the repatriation of Justice T. Vinod Kumar, Judge of the Madras High Court, to his parent High Court, the High Court for the State of Telangana.
The recommendation was made at the Collegium meeting held on September 28, 2026, in view of Justice Kumar's impending retirement on November 16, 2026.
Justice Kumar was transferred from the Telangana High Court to the Madras High Court in June 2025.
He has been serving as a Judge of the Madras High Court since the transfer.
The Collegium, in its statement, said that considering his "ensuing retirement" on November 16, 2026, it had recommended his repatriation to his parent High Court.
Justice Kumar was appointed as a Judge of the Telangana High Court in 2019.
He was subsequently transferred to the Madras High Court in June 2025.

stories.headline: Chief Justice of Karnataka HC constitutes panel of judges to examine feasibility for establishing Bench for coastal/Malnad districts
stories.title: Chief Justice of Karnataka HC constitutes panel of judges to examine feasibility for establishing Bench for coastal/Malnad districts
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'chief justice' in title weight 42
article_sentences: The Chief Justice of the High Court of Karnataka on Tuesday constituted a high-level committee comprising three judges to examine the feasibility of establishing a Circuit Bench/Permanent Bench of the court in the State’s coastal or Malnad region.
According to an official notification issued by the High Court’s Registrar General, the committee will consist of Justices Anu Sivaraman, S.G. Pandit, and Mohammad Nawaz.

The committee will “verify the feasibility of establishment of High Court Circuit Bench/Permanent Bench at Mangaluru/Udupi (Coastal Karnataka region)/Shivamogga/Chikkamagaluru/Kodagu-Madikeri/Hassan/Davanagere/Uttara Kannada districts after consulting all the stakeholders and submit a report”, the notification stated.

The demand for a permanent Bench in the coastal region has been a major political and legal talking point for years led by the Mangaluru Bar Association and the Coastal High Court Bench Agitation Committee.

The advocates and political leaders from the coastal districts repeatedly citing the logistical challenges and expenses involved in travelling to Bengaluru for legal proceedings before the High Court as a reason for a Bench at their doorstep.
Recently, it was reported that the authorities have indicated that a 50,000 sq.
facility at the old Deputy Commissioner’s office in Mnagaluru is available to house the Circuit Bench.
However, the Advocates’ Association, Bengaluru, formally opposed the move for a Bench in the coastal region while terming it as “premature” and lacking an empirical basis.

The AAB claimed that another Bench, in addition to the existing permanent Benches at Dharwad and Kalaburagi, would dilute the High Court’s institutional unity and warned that fragmenting the High Court could harm consistency in judicial administration.

stories.headline: From omission to Asiad gold: How Shafali Verma transformed her game
stories.title: From omission to Asiad gold: How Shafali Verma transformed her game
stories.summary: In November 2024, when Shafali Verma was dropped from the India team for its ODI tour of Australia, she hid the news from her father who was hospitalised with a heart attack a few days earlier. When she finally mustered the courage to tell him, Sanjeev, who introduced her to the sport and power hitting, sat silently for a few seconds before perking up. “He told me, ‘koi baat nahi, abhi aur bhi mehnat karenge’ [don’t worry, we’ll work even harder],” Verma had told Forbes India in an earlier interview. “I believe that when the going gets tough, gardan neeche karke chupchap kaam karte jao [put your head down and keep working quietly].”Two years on, Verma’s conviction has been vindicated as she has embarked on one of the most prolific phases of her career. It started in October 2024, when the 22-year-old earned a surprise recall to the ODI side, on a stage no less than the World Cup, despite not being part of the original 15-member squad. Coming in as a replacement for injured opener Pratika Rawal at the semifinal stage, Verma delivered an all-round masterclass in the final, capping her comeback with the Player of the Match award in November 2025 and celebrating her feat with her first vacation thereafter—a trip to Bali. But that was just the beginning.In her eight-year international career, Year 2026 has been Verma’s most prolific in T20Is, the format that she has long made her own with her batting blitzkrieg. By the end of the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan’s Aichi-Nagoya, where India won gold, Verma became the year’s highest run-scorer in the format, with 863 runs from 24 matches and a strike rate (runs per 100 balls) of 162.83, the highest among those from Test-playing nations.Seven of her 21 half-centuries in T20Is have come this year, along with a 49-ball century in the Asian Games semi-final—her first in white-ball cricket. The knock made Verma the first centurion in the history of the multi-sport event, where she also finished as the leading run-scorer and the only woman player to strike at over 200.“From the time I started playing cricket and realised that T20 is my favourite format, my dream was to hit a hundred. When the moment finally arrived, and I raised my bat and helmet, bachpan se aaj tak jitna hard work kiya tha, sab yaad aa gaya [I was reminded of all the hard work I have done since my childhood],” Verma told Forbes India in an interview upon her return to India. “I have waited for this for a long time.”Also Read: The innings after the World Cup final starts from zero: Shafali VermaSECOND INNINGSAt the heart of Verma’s turnaround, a Shafali 2.0 if you will, lies a more measured approach to shot-making: Aggressive, yet patient. Her 78-ball 87 in the ODI World Cup final is a telling example, where she went 20 balls without hitting a boundary before snapping out of the streak with a six. In five of her last eight matches—in the Asia Cup and at the Asian Games—Verma, an explosive opener, batted deep into the middle overs, negotiating a field spread beyond the 30-yard circle and packed with boundary riders that limited her natural, aerial game.“In these last two tournaments, she has played past the 10th over more often than not. Now you don’t see the old Shafali where she would frequently move away from the stumps [to manufacture a shot]. There’s a sense of calmness to her game as opposed to the earlier restlessness to score,” says Mithali Raj, former India captain and now a commentator. “Once you hit that level of understanding of your game, you cannot go back to your old self, you only want to keep going up a level.”Verma learnt to play on the attack from childhood, when her father set out to mould her into an aggressive opener. Initially, her shots wouldn’t travel far, but practising with heavier, wet leather balls helped her build strength and distance. While she made her international debut in 2019, at 15, it was with her heroics at the T20 World Cup in Australia the following year—when she steered India to the final as the team’s highest run-getter—that she grabbed the headlines. Ever since, her slam-bang game received widespread admiration and served her well as well. “From 2019 till about 2021, I only used to think of sixes. And that approach worked,” she says. “But after that, I started to get out in crucial matches.”For example, Verma was dismissed for 11 in the final of the Commonwealth Games at Birmingham in 2022, a match India narrowly lost to Australia by 9 runs; for 9 in the semifinal of the T20 World Cup in 2023, where Australia once again scraped past India by 5 runs; and aggregated 97 from four matches in the 2024 edition of the tournament in Dubai, where India failed to make it beyond the group stage. “For a long time, I felt I was lagging somewhere. It was after the 2024 World Cup in Dubai that I realised what needed to be worked on,” adds Verma. Soon after, she was axed from the ODI side too.THE ALL-ROUNDERWhen a young player gets dropped from a side, says Ashwani Kumar, a former Haryana player and Verma’s childhood coach, they tend to fall into a negative spiral. Not Verma, says Kumar, who has seen Verma since the time she landed up at his off-season camp in Rohtak at age 12. “She is the type who gears up to improve and fight back on merit. It reflects her mental make-up.”Out of the national team, Verma dived right into training, played domestic cricket for Haryana to iron the creases in her batting, while also sitting for special sessions with dieticians to improve her fitness. But the reset wasn’t merely physical. While she spent hours at the nets, training herself to play along the ground instead of looking to loft every shot, she also recalibrated her mind—sometimes through sessions with sports psychologists that the HCA had assigned to her and sometimes on her own.“Even during my free time at home, I would be running scenarios in my head where I should take singles if the ball wasn’t within hitting range,” she says. “Earlier, I was quite young and I didn’t know how to control my mind—so, while I had the skills, I lacked the mindset. The first step to rectifying it was acceptance. Then, through 2025, I worked very hard on my mindset.”The ability to work the ball for singles and twos has now opened up for Verma access to the entire ground, says Raj, the highest run-scorer in women’s cricket (till Smriti Mandhana recently overtook her in the Asian Games). “She is so good from the long off to the long on region—there are hardly any shots in the area that she’s mistimed in recent times,” she says. “Along with that, when you are able to play glides to the third man or flicks on the legside, it means you have upgraded your skills with low-risk shots. That's the reason she's able to play into the middle overs and if she continues like this, we’ll perhaps see her reaching those 100s more often.”Verma’s purple patch with the bat seems to be rubbing off on her bowling as well. In a recent media roundtable, she mentioned she enjoys her bowling more than batting as “it just takes one ball to get out in batting, while, with bowling, you get a chance to come back”. If she has a growing love for bowling, her recent statistics prove that bowling, too, loves her right back. Verma grabbed two key wickets in the triumphant ODI World Cup final against South Africa—of Sune Luus and Marizane Kapp—in what was only the sixth time she had bowled in 31 ODIs she had played till then; 12 of her 22 wickets in T20Is have also come this year.TWO TO TANGOPeople who’ve seen Verma from close quarters also sense an uptick in her fielding, which earlier was lagging her batting. She says she has learnt the trick to good fielding—of enjoying it. “I’ve worked on my fitness, I’m getting good reflexes,” she adds. And it’s evident from the way she’s been able to run in the deep, and from one end to the other after every over.Raj speaks about Verma’s new-found fielding chops, as does Jonathan Batty, the head coach of Delhi Capitals (DC), the franchise Verma plays for in the WPL (Women’s Premier League). “She has now developed into a fielder whom we rely on in the deep to take the catches. She dives around as well as anyone in the field,” says Batty.The former English first-class cricketer—who has seen the batter since the inaugural season in 2023, when Verma was lapped up by the side for Rs2 crore—also speaks about how Verma, a quick learner, imbibed from Meg Lanning, former Australia captain and seven-time World Cup winner who skippered the team for the first three seasons and opened the batting with her.While they were a picture of contrasts in terms of their career phases—Verma at its start and Lanning at the fag end—“it seemed to us that Shafali very quickly started to observe how Meg went about her business. There was more accuracy and precision in the way she would go about her practice,” says Batty. Eventually, it added clarity to her decision-making in shot selection: While Plan A is always to go for the big hits, it helped Verma develop Plan B, C, Ds, what have you, to minimise risks in her game and play on for longer.In its fourth season in 2026, Verma became only the second Indian after national captain Harmanpreet Kaur, and the fourth overall, to breach the 1,000-run-mark in the tournament. (Lanning—who has left DC for the UP Warriorz in the last season—is one among the two foreign players on the list.) “Once your adrenaline gets going, it’s difficult, as a batter, to bring it down. What Meg did was to keep Shafali in the moment. We would see her talk to Shafali after she’d hit a ball out of the ground,” says Batty.He adds: “Their dynamics was really interesting because Meg seemed to play with more freedom around Shafali—she became a bit more Shafali-like and Shafali became a little Meg-like in the way they structured their innings. It worked great for DC, and I see the same for Team India where Shafali and Smriti [Mandhana] play the perfect foil to each other.”Verma had earlier told Forbes India that Mandhana had taught her the importance of taking singles and getting to the non-striker’s end, allowing her to bide her time when the going got tough. The lesson appears to have paid off as the two are now the first set of openers in T20Is to have tallied 4,000-plus runs, with an over-1,000-run lead over UAE’s Esha Oza and Theertha Satish, who come second.BRAND GAMEThe transformation of Verma has not only reshaped her game, but has also strengthened her standing beyond the field. Her endorsement portfolio has grown 3x, from three before the ODI World Cup to 10 at present and includes the likes of global biggies like Nike and Google, while her revenues have climbed from Rs20 lakh per day per brand to somewhere between Rs60 lakh and Rs75lakh now, experts estimate. About half of these are long-term deals spanning between two and four years.“We're working to go from the prodigy narrative to the fact that she is a strong stakeholder in the Indian team. We want to position her as someone who is here for the long run,” says Himanshu Sharma, head of consulting and talent, JSW Sports, which manages the player. While the World Cup win has brought a windfall for the women’s cricket team, with brand deals pouring in, Verma’s story has a distinct edge, as she found herself in the spotlight despite not being part of the squad. “It has skyrocketed her image from just a 22-year-old to someone who was mature enough to come in and perform on the biggest stage,” adds Sharma.While her non-metro background can be an anchor for brands wanting to foray beyond metros, like fintechs, with her urban choices like love for cars, watches and fashion, she could bridge the India-Bharat divide. “Not too many sportspersons have come from tier 2 and 3 towns to become national stars. The only cricketer to do so in recent times is MS Dhoni. But that connect didn’t happen at the first go, it happened over time and because of his performance, his leadership qualities, his big-match prowess,” says Santosh N, partner, D&P Advisory, a valuation services firm. “Dhoni has shown that the template exists, and that performance is key to it.”With her game in the past year, Verma seems to have put that foundation firmly in place. Says Raj, considered to be one of the greats of the game: “I like that there is a consistency in the way in which she has been starting her innings. It means she is investing in repeating what has been working for her. That, for me, is an evolution of her and shows she's given a lot of thought to how she can go about.”With eight years of international cricket behind her, and already a World Cup in her kitty, it’s easy to forget Verma is only 22 and has decades ahead. What does she do in the years ahead to keep the momentum going? “I would never want to see her lose the aggressive streak because, with that, she does what few batters can do: Scare the living daylights out of the bowlers,” says Batty. “The key to staying ahead of the curve is to stay hungry—the really good players are always hungry.”Verma knows it well. Barely a fortnight after her ODI World Cup triumph, she had told Forbes India: “The next innings starts from zero.” And, despite her fairytale run, chances are she is rolling up her sleeves and taking guard for the next innings.

stories.title: Tata Trusts’ proposal could pave way for merger of Tata’s two iPhone manufacturing units
stories.summary: Tata Trusts advisor FarokhSubedar said TESS has the right to buy the balance 40 per cent shares
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tata Trusts’ proposal to keep Tata Sons private could lead to a merger of its two iPhone manufacturing units, Tata Electronics Systems Solutions Private Ltd (TESS) and Tata Electronics Products and Solutions Private Ltd.
TESS (formerly known as Wistron Infocomm Manufacturing India) owns 60 per cent stake in device maker Tata Electronics Products and Solutions Private Ltd ( formerly Pegatron Technology India Ltd).
Tata Trusts advisor.
Farokh Subedar said TESS has the right to buy the balance 40 per cent shares.
“ In a year’s time or so once it becomes 100 per cent subsidiary of this particular company (TESS), it can also get merged.
It will immediately add another ₹60,000 crore of income,” Subedar told reporters.

On Monday, Tata Trusts proposed a merger of Tata Electronics Systems Solutions Private Ltd (TESS) and Tata Consulting Engineers (TCE) with Tata Sons to keep the holding company outside ambit of RBI’s non-banking finance company -upper layer category (NBFC-UL).
Tata Trusts is hopeful that the merger will keep Tata Sons outside the purview of RBI’s regulatory framework for NBFC-UL.
It also believes that new investments by the holding company will not change the status.
Subedar said TESS has a turnover of over ₹60,000 crore and an asset size which keeps us below the 90 per cent cap applicable to a core investment company.
Tata Trusts did not respond to queries on steps involved in merger plan and risks involved in the process.
In 2023, Tata group acquired manufacturing facility of Wistron India which had faced labour unrest and plant shutdown.

stories.headline: Foreign Secretary flags concerns over US Russia sanctions law to US lawmakers
stories.title: Foreign Secretary flags concerns over US Russia sanctions law to US lawmakers
stories.summary: There are indications that the SRIA may be used as a leverage in the ongoing India-US negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement, sources said
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri conveyed India’s concerns over the recent Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA) – that empowers US administration to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on imports from countries buying Russian oil – to a visiting US Congressional delegation and noted that it may affect bilateral relationship and the global energy market, the Ministry of External Affairs has said.
“At the meeting (on Sunday), various issues of bilateral interest were discussed.

Foreign Secretary conveyed our concerns in regard to the SRIA legislation, as far as the kind of implications it would have on the bilateral relationship as also the international market,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a media briefing on Tuesday.

While the SRIA empowers the US President to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on top buyers of Russian energy, including India, it does not lead to an automatic imposition of 100 per cent tariff on Indian goods.
There are indications that the SRIA may be used as a leverage in the ongoing India-US negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement, sources said.

Commerce & Industry Minister Piyush Goyal is visiting the US this week to attend a G20 trade ministers’ meeting and hold discussions with his counterparts on the pact, which has gone through prolonged discussions amid considerable tariff uncertainty this year.
India has been closely assessing the implications of the legislation as it remains a major buyer of Russian crude.
New Delhi has maintained that its energy purchases are guided by energy security and market considerations.

stories.summary: The centre will be established at a total cost of ₹82.80 lakh for a period of three years, with Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) serving as the implementing agency

article_sentences: The Karnataka Government has approved the establishment of Global Technology Centres (GTCs) in Belagavi and Hubballi to expand Karnataka’s technology growth beyond Bengaluru to different parts of the State, said Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, Information Technology, Biotechnology, and E-Governance.
The Government has approved the establishment of the GTC with plug-and-play facilities across approximately 10,000 sq.
at Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) in Belagavi.
The centre will be established at a total cost of ₹82.80 lakh for a period of three years, with Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) serving as the implementing agency.
The Government has also approved the GTC across approximately 10,000 sq.
at the Hubballi.
IT Park, on rent-free premises.
The centre will entail a total expenditure of ₹5.80 crore over a period of three years, comprising ₹4.90 crore towards capital expenditure and ₹0.90 crore towards operational expenditure.
“Karnataka’s technology capabilities cannot be limited to Bengaluru alone.
There is a need to nurture the talent and entrepreneurship emerging across different regions of the State.
The establishment of Global Technology Centres in Belagavi and Hubballi will create new opportunities for the youth, startups and technology-driven enterprises in North Karnataka,” Kharge said.

The centres are being established under the Local Economy Accelerator Programme (LEAP), aimed at providing technology talent, startups and entrepreneurship with the necessary infrastructure and opportunities locally beyond Bengaluru.
